item.title: Border Biennial 2026 invited regional artists to imagine the border
item.dc:creator: Daniel Perez
item.description:
More than 70 works explore the border through sculpture, painting, photography and other media in an exhibition celebrating artists from the Paso del Norte region.

The post Border Biennial 2026 invited regional artists to imagine the border appeared first on El Paso Matters.
item.content:encoded:
Regional artists are showcasing their creativity and love of the area during the Border Biennial 2026 that opened this weekend at the El Paso Museum of Art and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez, Mexico. This year’s theme is “Imagining the Border.”

“We can read the border, we can drive the border, we can walk the border, we can paint the border, but to imagine the border is something different,” said Edward Hayes Jr., director of the El Paso museum. “It’s very open-ended.”

Hayes sat down to talk about the exhibition after a walk-through of the 7,000-square-foot Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Gallery, the temporary home to more than 70 paintings, sculptures, ceramics, tapestries, jewelry and photography and other pieces of art.

He said some of the selected artists focused on everyday life while others took a more dramatic view and submitted immigration-centered works. Similar art will be part of the exhibit at the Juárez museum, where the exhibit is called Bienal Fronteriza.  

“At the end of the day, this is a celebration of incredible creativity that exists along the border,” Hayes said. The opening weekend included special celebrations at both museums.

Christian Diego Diego, director of the Juárez art museum, said the exhibition serves as a benchmark for collaborative effort and exposure for border artists and their creative community.

He said his museum, located in the ProNaF zone, would present 60 pieces of art in its Sala Circular, or Circular Gallery. It would have the same types of art from most of the same artists featured in the El Paso museum.

Diego said these activities keep regional art production popular and relevant, and gives artists the space and support they need to grow. The fact that this event, which started in 2008, continues is deeply meaningful to him.

“It allows us to build upon the legacy of everyone who launched this project while continuing to open our museum’s doors to the region’s vibrant artistic community,” Diego said in an email to El Paso Matters.

These kinds of events create a special opportunity to ground the larger “frontera” region as a critically important center of art production of the highest level, said Eduardo Diaz, retired director of the Smithsonian Latino Center in Washington, D.C.

Diaz said that this exhibit along with two other significant art showcases in November, Latino Art Now! and SUTURA, will reinforce the notion that El Paso-Juárez is a core art area.

“El Paso and Cd. Juárez are about to send a powerful message to the larger art world that will resonate for years to come,” Diaz said in an email response to El Paso Matters.”

Hayes said he expects more than 25,000 visitors will see the Border Biennial on the El Paso side before it closes May 2, 2027. He added that the museum, located at 1 Arts Festival Plaza, might extend the run as it did with the 2024 Border Biennial if there is interest. The Juárez part of the exhibition will close in early February 2027.     

The call for artists generated more than 130 applications. Organizers, who asked that the artists be from within a 300 mile radius of El Paso-Juárez, whittled that down to 31 artists and two artists collectives from Texas, Arizona, New Mexico and Chihuahua, Mexico. For many of them, this will be their first big exhibit.

The lead Border Biennial curators were Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales. In a prepared statement, Morales said the selection process allowed them to encounter emerging artists whose proposals addressed contemporary concerns and questions about the desert borderlands “across political, affective, communal and personal registers.”

Among the selected artists is Angel Cabrales, an associate professor of art at the University of Texas at El Paso. His focus is on sculpture. He previously participated in the 2013 and 2019 Border Biennials when he worked for other institutions in Texas and Illinois.

His entries are “The Rosary of Eagle Pass,” which he made in 2025, and “Five Lights” from 2024.

The 26-foot-long rosary uses metal-encased orange “beads” that represent the orange buoys that the Texas government placed in the Rio Grande at Eagle Pass, Texas, to deter migrants from entering the state.

“Five Lights” is an American flag made from steel to simulate the border wall. The portion with the stars is replaced with the Department of Homeland Security emblem. Beneath it are 12 2-inch acrylic cubes filled with discarded personal belongings of migrants. Above the flag are four very bright lights shining down into a visitors’ sightline.

It is called “Five Lights” as a reference to a psychological torture technique used in “Chain of Command: Part II,” a sixth-season episode of “Star Trek: The Next Generation.”

In it, an interrogator shows a prisoner four lights, asks for the number of lights, and punishes the prisoner when he answers correctly. The interrogator insists there are five lights as he tries to force the prisoner to surrender mentally and emotionally. A similar technique was used in the George Orwell novel “1984,” but fingers were used instead of lights.

He said the exhibit’s art pieces show the level of love artists have for the area and how much they want to share that love with others.

“I think that’s the greatest thing,” Cabrales said.

Michael Reyes, senior curator at the El Paso Museum of Art, said he was amazed by how the artists had different visions of the border. He said some common threads included laborers, surveillance and the border wall.

In spite of the more confrontational pieces, Reyes said artists still found beauty in the natural landscape. In general, he believes the exhibit lifts up and showcases regional art.

Hayes, the El Paso museum director, said the pandemic and regional challenges of shipping art between the two countries led to the cancellations of the event starting in 2018. The program resumed in 2024.

He said the event generated interest from the New York Times, which published a story about the Border Biennial in April 2024 as part of the newspaper’s museums special section.

For those who choose not to cross the border, Hayes said exhibit organizers are thinking about possible virtual activities in 2027 that would allow patrons to see Border Biennial pieces at the others’ museum.    

The city of El Paso Museums and Cultural Affairs Department, the Secretaría de Cultura de México (Ministry of Culture of Mexico) and the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature) helped organize the Border Biennial.  

The exhibition’s supporters include the Mellon Foundation, the Texas Commission on the Arts, the El Paso Museum of Art Foundation, and the city of El Paso Museums and Cultural Affairs Department.

2026 Border Biennial

The 2026 Border Biennial / Bienal Fronteriza features 31 artists and two collectives representing Arizona, Chihuahua, New Mexico and Texas.The biennial  opened this weekend at the El Paso Museum of Art and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez, Mexico. The exhibit at the El Paso museum will remain on display through May 2, 2027.

  • Where: Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Gallery, El Paso Museum of Art, 1 Arts Festival Plaza Downtown
  • Hours: 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday; 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sunday. Closed Monday and Tuesday. 
  • Admission: Free.

Artists selected for this year’s exhibit include:

item.title: El Paso school districts to retrofit, purchase buses to meet state’s new seat belt law
item.dc:creator: Claudia Lorena Silva
item.description:
Texas school districts have three years to ensure all their school buses are equipped with lap-and-shoulder seat belts, costing the districts millions.

The post El Paso school districts to retrofit, purchase buses to meet state’s new seat belt law appeared first on El Paso Matters.
item.content:encoded:
Safety is top of mind for Eddy Harris every morning as the sun rises over the horizon and he inspects the yellow school bus that will transport dozens of students to and from school that day.

“You go in, and you check your tires, you check your oil, you check your transmission fluid. You know you have to do these checks daily to make sure when your bus get out there, it doesn’t break down,” said Harris, an Ysleta Independent School District bus driver and Gulf War veteran.

Harris and his fellow drivers have to traverse unpredictable traffic, adapt to changing weather conditions and adhere to the rules of the road while monitoring a bus full of occasionally rowdy students.

“You have to have a lot of patience,” YISD bus driver Henry Vasquez said calmly as he sat at the district’s transportation hub in the Lower Valley.

“It’s a big responsibility, but it’s very rewarding getting the kids to school and home safely,” added YISD bus driver Jaime Urenda.

YISD and school districts across the state are working to make school buses safer under a new Texas law that requires they be equipped with three-point seat belts that go over a passenger’s chest and lap by Sept. 1, 2029.

Currently, school buses only need two-point seat belts, which go over a passenger’s lap, if they were made on or after 2018.

Senate Bill 546 requires school districts to estimate the costs of installing three-point seat belts, present a report to the board, and send information to the Texas Education Agency on any potential budget limitations before June 2027.

The bill, which was passed during the 2025 state Legislature, was introduced in response to the 2024 school bus crash in Bastrop County that led to the deaths of a pre-kindergarten student and the passenger of another vehicle.

With no state dollars attached to the legislation, many El Paso school district officials worry it will create financial strain on their already tight budgets if Texas lawmakers don’t provide funding before the deadline.

For a large school bus fleet, the cost of complying with the new seat belt requirements can become significant, particularly when combined with the need to replace aging buses and maintain the existing fleet,” YISD Director of Transportation Rosario Fernandez said.

“Without dedicated state funding, these expenditures would have to compete with other district priorities and the cost of complying with the new seat belt requirements would have to be considered within the district’s existing financial resources,” Fernandez added.

The El Paso Independent School District, the largest in the region, plans to install three-point seat belts into 140 of its buses, which will cost an estimated $7.15 million and be split into two phases

Socorro and Ysleta school district officials say they plan to replace buses that don’t have the proper restraints rather than retrofitting them, partially because the upgrades could void their warranties. 

The Socorro Independent School District plans to start by entering an agreement, which was approved in June as part of its budget, with Highland Fleet — a Massachusetts-based company that specializes in providing electric buses to schools — to add 25 buses to its electric vehicle fleet. The Ysleta district plans to purchase 75 school buses using maintenance tax notes, which serve as long-term loans.

An estimated 27,300 students enrolled in El Paso’s three largest school districts ride the bus every day. About 8,000 of them attend EPISD, 7,000 attend SISD and 12,300 attend YISD.

Most El Paso schools provide transportation to students who live outside a campus’ two-mile radius or those who would have to cross dangerous roads to walk to school. The state gives school districts additional funding to offer transportation to these students, as well as special education and homeless students.

In 2025, EPISD split its district into four transportation zones and began allowing students to take the bus to any school within their zone. This was a part of the district’s plan to close several underutilized schools due to declining enrollment, which left some students further away from their neighborhood campuses.

School districts also rely on their buses to take students on field trips, for certain extracurricular activities and for competitions that require travel.

Safety concerns have kept some parents, such as Angela Dickson, whose 11-year-old daughter attends Don Haskins PK-8 School, from using the bus to get their children to and from school.

“She’s only been on them during school field trips. The seat belts is just another reason it makes me uneasy for them to travel on the bus daily,” Dickson said.

For  Genevieve Medrano, the school bus has been the most reliable way to ensure her daughter Naeli, 10, gets to Pebble Hills Elementary School. Medrano, who shares a car with her husband, said she doesn’t always have transportation available to take their daughter to school and welcomes the new seat belt requirements.

“It’s good because you never know if there’s going to be an accident and something can happen, and it’s better to be safe,” Medrano said.

Despite some parents’ concerns, school buses are safer than walking or riding in a car, according to the National Safety Council. The council supports the use of lap-and-shoulder seatbelts to make school buses safer, but did not

On average, there have been 108 school-bus-related fatalities a year in the U.S. between 2015 and 2024, only about 6% of which were school bus passengers. That is out of the 42,000 vehicle fatalities that happen every year.

New school buses

As the deadline to submit the TEA transportation reports neared, El Paso’s three largest school districts in May presented an update to their boards on what it would take to comply with SB 546.

SISD has 275 buses in its fleet, 129 of which already have three-point seat belts. The district estimated it will cost $3.3 million to retrofit the remainder of its buses with the required restraints and $22.9 million to replace them completely.

Only 30 of YISD’s 226 buses have the required seat belts. Officials estimate it will cost $4.8 million to retrofit nearly 200 buses and $31.7 million to replace them.

EPISD has about 260 buses, and less than half have three-point seat belts. District officials did not say how much it would cost to replace their buses during the meeting, but have said they plan to auction off older buses and potentially use bond funding to pay to install seat belts. The district plans to ask voters in May 2027 to approve a nearly half-a-billion-dollar bond proposal to upgrade air conditioners and make improvements throughout its campuses.

YISD and SISD have already started work on acquiring new school buses, in part to meet SB 546’s requirements.

The YISD school board voted Aug. 12 to authorize the issuance of $65 million in maintenance tax notes for facility improvements and to purchase 75 school buses. YISD officials said the cost of the new buses will range from $160,000 to $180,000 each depending on the size.

This comes as the district is trying to slash expenses to avoid layoffs after adopting a budget that nearly depleted its reserves.

Fernandez, Ysleta’s transportation director, said some of the district’s buses are over 30 years old and use parts that are difficult to find or need to be custom made.

“It’s really not about just retrofitting older buses, but it’s actually moving in the direction of making sure that these new buses that we get are equipped and that they meet all safety requirements, and I think at the end it’s something that’ll be good for the district,” Fernandez said.

YISD bus driver Ray Morales said the district’s buses haven’t had any major issues, but have been affected by regular wear and tear.

“There’s nothing really wrong with them. It’s just, they’re outdated,” Morales said. “We use these buses every day, anywhere from six to eight hours a day. Things are bound to happen. There’s going to be leaks, there’s going to be flats because we don’t give them the rest.”

SISD, the first in the region to transition to a renewable energy source for transportation, plans to lease 25 electric school buses to add to its fleet.

The district began using 25 electric buses in 2024 after receiving over $9.8 million from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Clean School Bus Funding program to build charging stations and purchase the vehicles.

Instead of purchasing new buses, SISD will contract with Highland Fleet to lease its buses at a rate of $18,000 a year for each vehicle.

Under the contract, Highland Fleet will install the charging stations and reimburse the district for any parts or repairs that are needed. This will save SISD nearly $5 million over the next 10 years compared to operating traditional diesel buses, according to the presentation given by the company in May.

SISD’s Assistant Superintendent of Administrative Services Enrique Herrera said 20 of the new electric buses will be used by special education students, who have their own dedicated routes and vehicles.

“We’ve gotten a lot of great feedback from not only the bus drivers but the students,” Herrera said.

“Part of that idea is to accommodate the sensitivity of our special needs students. (The buses) make no noise, and they provide a better experience for our students as well,” he added.

Fernandez said YISD isn’t looking into buying electric buses because of the time it takes to charge them and the additional investment needed to build charging stations. But officials said they may consider other energy efficient options, such as natural gas or propane.

“It’s just the infrastructure, the charging stations, the whole layout. I think it’s just a little bit more than just buying the bus,” Fernandez said.

No matter what kind of vehicle they will be driving, YISD’s bus drivers said getting students to school, making connections with their young passengers and contributing to their education makes the job worthwhile.

“I love to be a bus driver because every morning when you receive all the students, they have some big smiles,” YISD bus driver Gabriela Rojas said.

The post El Paso school districts to retrofit, purchase buses to meet state’s new seat belt law appeared first on El Paso Matters.

item.title: Superheroes Health Fair helps El Paso families start the school year healthy
item.dc:creator: Special to El Paso Matters
item.description:
Texas Tech Physicians of El Paso event connects more than 300 children and families with healthcare, backpacks and community resources

The post Superheroes Health Fair helps El Paso families start the school year healthy appeared first on El Paso Matters.
item.content:encoded:
More than 300 El Paso children and their families got some help preparing for the new school year this summer — from pediatricians, community organizations and a few superheroes.

The Superheroes Health Fair at Texas Tech Physicians of El Paso at Alberta brought families together for a Saturday of health screenings, sports physicals, backpacks and other resources, while costumed superheroes, music, face painting and activities helped turn a trip to the doctor into a community celebration.

Hosted by the General Pediatrics Outpatient Division in partnership with El Paso Health, the July 11 event brought together 25 community partners to connect families with services ranging from dental screenings to mental health resources.

For Dr. Maria Theresa Villanos, division chief of ambulatory pediatrics and medical director of the pediatric clinic, the turnout showed the need for accessible healthcare combined with an atmosphere children and their families could enjoy.

“It was packed,” Villanos said. “The families enjoyed popcorn, music, face painting, photos at the photo booth and the appearance of the superheroes, plus raffle prizes and healthy lifestyle counseling.”

Getting El Paso children ready for school

For families, the health fair offered an opportunity to take care of some important back-to-school needs in one place.

Pediatricians and clinic staff performed more than 30 physicals and conducted Texas Health Steps checkups, well-child visits and sports physicals. Children had their height, weight and body mass index measured, while families received personalized counseling about healthy lifestyles.

Most checkups were covered by Medicaid or private insurance. Uninsured children, including those who were not already Texas Tech Physicians of El Paso patients, could receive sports physicals for $25.

El Paso Health also sponsored 300 backpacks for children attending the event, adding another back-to-school resource for local families.

The combination of medical care and family activities was intentional. While parents connected with health professionals and community organizations, children could meet costumed superheroes, have their faces painted, take photos and enjoy music and popcorn.

The result was part health fair and part neighborhood gathering — and an opportunity to make preventive care more approachable for children.

El Paso organizations come together

The health fair also showed what can happen when healthcare providers and community organizations work together to meet families where they are.

Twenty-five community partners participated, transforming the Alberta clinic into a one-stop wellness hub. Participants included the Foster School of Medicine departments of psychiatry and obstetrics and gynecology, the Hunt School of Dental Medicine and the Child Psychiatry Access Network.

Dr. Julianna M. Khoury-Martin, assistant professor and chair of community outreach for the Pediatrics Ambulatory Division, said bringing those resources together was central to the event.

“We were very excited to see the community come together for children’s health in preparation for this school year,” Khoury-Martin said. “The capacity attendance speaks volumes, especially after the event’s hiatus following COVID.”

For Texas Tech Physicians of El Paso, events such as the Superheroes Health Fair extend the work its pediatricians do every day into the community they serve.

The Alberta pediatric clinic is staffed by board-certified pediatricians and offers same-day appointments and a 24-hour parent hotline, providing El Paso families with access to care beyond special community events.

The fair also strengthened the connection between Texas Tech Health El Paso and the community where its students and resident physicians train. As the region’s only independent academic health sciences center, the university gives future healthcare professionals opportunities to learn firsthand about the needs of El Paso and Borderplex families while helping expand access to care and health resources.

Organizing an event for hundreds of children required its own team behind the scenes. Interim Department of Pediatrics Chair Dr. Manuel de la Rosa and administrator Lori Ruthledge provided support for the event, while clinic manager Alex Lopez and head nurse Cecilia Lindsey helped coordinate the effort alongside volunteers, vendors and community partners.

But for the families who walked through the clinic doors that Saturday, the result was much simpler: an opportunity to get children ready for school, connect with local health resources and make a visit to the doctor a little more fun.

More than 30 physicals were completed, 300 backpacks found their way into children’s hands and hundreds of El Paso families left with information and resources to help them begin the school year healthier.

And for at least one Saturday in El Paso, healthcare really did come with a cape.
